title: Question (Section 3, implicit representation for speed $2^{O(n\log n)}$)
statement_text: Is it possible that hereditary families with speed $f(n) \leq 2^{O(n \log n)}$ always admit an implicit representation of size $O(n^{1/2} \log n)$?
context_text: A family $\mathcal{F}$ of graphs is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs; $\mathcal{F}_n$ is the set of members of $\mathcal{F}$ with $n$ vertices, and the speed of $\mathcal{F}$ is $f(n)=|\mathcal{F}_n|$. An implicit representation of size $\ell(n)$ of $\mathcal{F}_n$ is a function assigning a label of $\ell(n)$ bits to each vertex of any graph $G\in\mathcal{F}_n$ so that the adjacency between any two vertices is determined by their labels (the labeling need not be efficiently computable); equivalently, there is a universal graph on $2^{\ell(n)}$ vertices containing every member of $\mathcal{F}_n$ as an induced subgraph. Necessarily $\ell(n)\ge\log_2|\mathcal{F}_n|/n$. Speed $2^{O(n\log n)}$ holds for many natural families, e.g. those whose vertices are points of a bounded-dimensional real space with adjacency determined by signs of bounded-degree polynomials (intersection graphs of segments or discs in the plane, for which economic implicit representations are not known). Hatami and Hatami showed that for every $\delta>0$ there are hereditary families with speed $f(n)\le 2^{O(n\log n)}$ for which any implicit representation requires labels of size at least $\Omega(n^{1/2-\delta})$, and asked whether the exponent $1/2$ can be improved. Alon proves that speed $f(n)\le 2^{(1/4-\varepsilon)n^2}$ already guarantees an implicit representation of size $O(n^{1-1/d}\log n)$ for some integer $d$ depending on $\varepsilon$, and asks whether $O(n^{1/2}\log n)$ always suffices in the $2^{O(n\log n)}$ speed range.
notes: Posed as an explicit question in Section 3 but without a labelled theorem environment; PDF source.
paper_title: Implicit representation of sparse hereditary families

title: Question (Section 3, implicit representation for speed $2^{n^{1+\varepsilon}}$)
statement_text: If the speed of a hereditary family satisfies $f(n) < 2^{n^{1+\varepsilon}}$ for a sufficiently small fixed $\varepsilon > 0$, is there always an implicit representation of size at most $O(n^{2/3} \log n)$?
context_text: A family $\mathcal{F}$ of graphs is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs; $\mathcal{F}_n$ is the set of members of $\mathcal{F}$ with $n$ vertices, and the speed of $\mathcal{F}$ is $f(n)=|\mathcal{F}_n|$. An implicit representation of size $\ell(n)$ of $\mathcal{F}_n$ is a function assigning a label of $\ell(n)$ bits to each vertex of any graph $G\in\mathcal{F}_n$ so that the adjacency between any two vertices is determined by their labels; equivalently, there is a universal graph on $2^{\ell(n)}$ vertices containing every member of $\mathcal{F}_n$ as an induced subgraph. Alon's main theorem: for any $\varepsilon>0$ there is an integer $d$ such that every hereditary family with speed $f(n)\le 2^{(1/4-\varepsilon)n^2}$ admits an implicit representation of size $O(n^{1-1/d}\log n)$, and for every $d>1$ this is tight up to the $\log n$ factor for some hereditary family. He asks whether tighter bounds hold when the speed grows more slowly: for speed $2^{O(n\log n)}$, whether $O(n^{1/2}\log n)$ always suffices (Hatami and Hatami showed $n^{1/2-\delta}$ may be needed there), and, as here, whether speed below $2^{n^{1+\varepsilon}}$ for a sufficiently small fixed $\varepsilon>0$ always allows labels of size $O(n^{2/3}\log n)$.
notes: Posed as an explicit question in Section 3 but without a labelled theorem environment; PDF source.
paper_title: Implicit representation of sparse hereditary families
